metadata.title: Newton's Third Law: Equal Forces on Two Bodies
metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.objective: Show two equal and opposite forces acting on two different bodies, and why they do not cancel while the accelerations differ by mass.
misconceptions: Action and reaction cancel because they are equal and opposite
The larger object exerts a larger force
expectedUnderstanding: A force pair is equal in magnitude and opposite in direction
The two forces act on two different bodies, so they are never added together
Each body's acceleration is its own force divided by its own mass
Mass changes acceleration, not the size of the force pair

primitives.text: One interaction, two bodies, two separate forces
The pair stays at 60 N; each acceleration is 60 divided by that body's mass.
Each body feels only the other's 60 N, so neither force cancels: mass changes a, not F.

checkpoints.title: Which body does each arrow belong to?
checkpoints.body: The red arrow is the force A exerts on B, so it is drawn inside B and points right. The blue arrow is the force B exerts on A, so it is drawn inside A and points left. One interaction, two forces, two different bodies.

checkpoints.title: Equal length
checkpoints.body: Both arrows are 60 N long. Predict first: if B were ten times heavier, would the red arrow be longer? Then move the mass sliders. The force arrows do not change, because third-law pairs are always equal.

checkpoints.title: Why they do not cancel
checkpoints.body: Forces cancel only when they act on the same body. Here each body carries exactly one horizontal force, so each net force is 60 N: A to the left, B to the right. The pair is equal and opposite, but it is never added together.

checkpoints.title: Mass enters through a, not F
checkpoints.body: Set one mass to 20 and the other to 90. The force arrows stay equal while the acceleration arrows become long and short in inverse proportion to mass, and the heavier block is drawn taller. Mass changes 60 divided by m, which is acceleration, not the force the other body feels.

narration.text: Two bodies in contact. A pushes B to the right; B pushes A to the left.
Both arrows are sixty newtons. Equal magnitude, opposite direction, and each one sits on a different body.
They never cancel, because cancellation needs two forces on the same body. Each body has just one horizontal force here.
Now change the masses. The force arrows stay put; the acceleration arrows change, because each body divides the same force by its own mass.
Lighter body, larger acceleration. The force pair is unchanged. Mass changes a, not F.

fallback.text: When body A pushes body B, body B pushes body A with a force equal in magnitude and opposite in direction. The two forces never cancel, because each acts on a different body: A feels only the push from B, and B feels only the push from A. If the forces are 60 N, then A accelerates at 60 divided by the mass of A and B accelerates at 60 divided by the mass of B, in opposite directions. Mass therefore changes the acceleration, not the size of the force pair; a heavier body does not push harder, it only accelerates less.

accessibility.alt: Two blocks in contact: a red arrow in B points right (A on B, 60 N), a blue arrow in A points left (B on A, 60 N). Acceleration arrows above them point opposite ways and lengthen as mass falls.
